Race and Racism in Hegel – An Analysis
M. A. R. Habib. Hegel and Empire: From Postcolonialism to Globalism. London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017. ISBN: 978-3-319-68411-6 (hbk). 164 pp. £49.99.
results.abstract: As the discipline of philosophy begins to come to terms with its entanglements in histories of colonialism, Eurocentrism and white supremacy, there is an increasing demand for scholarship that rigorously interrogates what these histories mean for the practice of philosophy today. WithHegel and Empire,M. A. R. Habib asks some of the important questions that emerge in this regard, in so far as they relate to Hegel’s philosophy and the legacy of Hegelian dialectics. In this sense it is, on paper, a welcome contribution to a growing literature which uses insights from critical race, postand de-colonial studies to rewrite the history of philosophy. However, and unfortunately, the book also represents a missed opportunity for a relevant intervention into this academic field since it fails to construct a compelling account of the possible relations between Hegel’s philosophy, the conceptions of empire and imperialism which we might find therein, and the realities and consequences of modern imperial domination and colonial exploitation. This could be excused if the primary purpose was to act as an introductory volume on Hegel and Eurocentrism and as a guide to further readings within post-Hegelian literature on this topic. Such is indeed the format indicated by the outline of the book since chapters which contain readings of Hegel’s writings (first and foremost the master–slave dialectic but also passages from the the lectures on the philosophy of world history, art and religion, including the infamous loose manuscript sheets on the geographic base of historical determinations) are paired with short summary chapters which delineate select responses from what might broadly be described as a ‘critical tradition’. What the strategy of fusing readings succeeds with, is to introduce the central and decisive question concerning the degree to which Eurocentrism can be conceived of as engrained within Hegel’s philosophy as a whole. The reader gets an introduction to (a) Susan BuckMorss’s and Andrew Cole’s respective ‘historical’ interpretations of the master– slave dialectic (in Buck-Morss’s Hegel, Haiti and Universal History 2009 and Cole’s The Birth of Theory (2014)), (b) Frantz Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952), and (c) Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s commentary on Hegel’s engagement with the Bhagavad Gita (from A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999).
